title: Writing jingles and 60-second spots
summary: Jingles were difficult but paid the bills while raising two boys, including a long run of commercials for Wegmans.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: There’s always an answer. I’m glad you moved on, you brought up jingles, because I wanted to spend a little time with that. It seems like another area of music that requires a certain approach, especially if it’s background music. And did you find that difficult to get used to?

Very difficult. Especially 60-second spots. You have to say it in 60 seconds but you also have to be able to cut that 60 down to 30 or a 20, or make it longer. I’ll say one thing, I should point out that all the time I was writing jazz with, you know, two young boys, two children and a wife, the way you survive is writing whatever you can. And the jingles and the industrial videos and all that stuff saves your life. But — and you don’t have to put your name on it. So it was a great way of supporting a family, but a lot of idiots out there, I mean the ignorance among the advertising agencies is incredible. The plop-plop-fizz- fizz, the Sammy Davis thing, that was a disaster. And you really have to think quickly on your feet. You really have to be sharp, and know all the different styles of music when you’re writing jingles. You have to know all of the styles. I did Wegman’s commercials for years, all of their commercials. And we had — I wrote the theme and then there was a Thanksgiving, there was an Easter, there was an October-fest and there was a — whatever season they were pushing, turkeys or whatever you know. And you would have to make it all work.
Well the next time I go into Wegman’s I’m going to say I know the guy who did all your commercials.
Yeah I did them for years, yeah. It was a good run. It was a nice account to have it really was.
